summary:
Space Tekong is a public web app for exploring NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky and investigating changes over time. Visitors select a sky region by coordinates, object name, or map position, choose observation dates and a wavelength preset or custom range, then load observations on demand or reopen shared results.

The Sky Viewer combines dated imagery, individual-exposure playback, blink/fade/two-color comparisons, and Gaia/WISE reference overlays. Analysis tools add brightness measurements across wavelength and time, explicit motion-candidate searches, official DR1 spectral-cube browsing, false-color RGB composites, and calibrated differences between independent exposures. Optional guided walkthroughs introduce the workflow without starting processing automatically.

Space Tekong makes astronomical data more approachable for students, educators, and citizen scientists while retaining observation times, quality flags, provenance, and coverage gaps. It helps people investigate possible changes and share their evidence, with clear distinctions between visual differences, candidate sources, and confirmed discoveries.
details:
What It Does

Space Tekong helps anyone explore NASA's SPHEREx infrared images and look for changes in the sky. Visitors can search for an object, enter sky coordinates, or choose a spot on the map. They can adjust the region size, dates, and infrared wavelength range, then load observations or open shared results.

A Simple Workflow

Free Exploration provides a sky map, object search, labels, and a Library. In SPHEREx mode, Regions loads and manages observations. Analysis brings four tools together for the selected region:

- Compare Images: Move between dates, play individual observations, or compare images using blink, fade, and two-color views. Users can also combine two image previews or display their differences.

- Brightness: Plot the available brightness measurements across infrared wavelengths or over time. Gaia and WISE overlays add information from other telescopes, including quality warnings.

- Motion Candidates: Start a separate search for possible moving objects, then inspect the images behind each candidate. Loading a region does not automatically start this search.

- Spectral Imaging: Browse NASA's official 102-channel infrared data, combine three channels into a false-color image, or request a calibrated difference between two separate observations. Each channel shows a different range of infrared light.

How It Works

The app finds matching SPHEREx observations and reads only the parts of NASA's public FITS files needed for the chosen region. Background workers align the images and keep their dates, source information, and quality flags. Completed results are stored so other visitors can reuse them. Users can follow progress and cancel or retry shared jobs.

Designed For Everyone

Optional guided walkthroughs introduce both modes through real actions. Users decide when to start processing. Shortcuts introduce the five challenge targets, and shareable links let people return to a view or discuss it with others. Our goal is to make real astronomy data easier for students, educators, and citizen scientists to explore in a browser.

Understanding The Results

Available dates do not always mean usable pixels. Some images combine observations from different times or wavelengths. The 102-channel data also combine observations over time, and blank channels stay blank. Image differences, brightness plots, and motion candidates are clues to investigate, not confirmed discoveries. Catalog labels do not prove that SPHEREx detected an object.

Tools And AI Assistance

We built the app with TypeScript, React, Aladin Lite, Python astronomy libraries, Cloudflare Workers and Containers, and Neon PostgreSQL with S3-compatible storage. ChatGPT and Claude assisted research, coding/debugging, and writing/editing.
